newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian cosmonauts talk to families from Mir.
newsitem.headline: Russian cosmonauts talk to families from Mir.

text.p: The Russian-U.S. crew aboard the crippled Mir space station enjoyed a rest day on Sunday and the four Russian cosmonauts spoke to their families in a 45-minute video link-up with Earth.

A spokesman at Korolyov Mission Control outside Moscow said all five men in orbit were well as they continued the week-long handover which began with the arrival of a two-man Russian relief crew last Thursday.

Two cosmonauts will head home on Thursday, leaving on board NATO physicist Michael Foale and the new two-man team, which is due to start dangerous repair work on August 20 to restore power lost in a collision nearly seven weeks ago.
"They are all well and everything is going fine," the spokesman said.
"Today was a rest day. The cosmonauts spoke to their families through a video link-up, all of them except Michael."

The spokesman did not say what the cosmonauts discussed with their families, who were brought to Mission Control for the video link-up. Reporters were not allowed inside and were given no access to the families.
Foale, 40, spoke at length to NASA officials in Houston by radio on Saturday, Russian space officials said. They gave no details of the conversation.

Commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, are due to return to Earth on Thursday, completing a six-month mission. They blasted off on February 10 and docked with Mir on February 12.

The worst moment of their ill-fated mission was the collision on June 25 in which a docking manoeuvre went wrong and a cargo craft punctured the Spektr module attached to Mir. It was the worst accident in Mir's 11 years in space.

Among other mishaps, an onboard fire broke out in February. After the collision, an unidentified liquid escaped into space and one of the crew caused a brief crisis by accidentally unplugging a vital computer, sending the station into a spin.
They have been dogged by problems with the power and oxygen supplies, and Tsibliyev suffered an irregular heartbeat brought on by stress.

The new team of commander Anatoly Solovyov, 49, and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov, 43, will try to fix the damage, including donning spacesuits to try to restore the power supply from the airless Spektr.

They are due to step outside the craft on September 3 to see how bad the hole in Spektr is. Russian officials have said they want Foale to take part in the spacewalk but NASA have not yet said if he will be allowed to do so.
The accidents have raised new questions about international cooperation with Russia in space.

But President Boris Yeltsin gave the space programme a boost on Friday by giving the green light to raising new credits to help Russia complete its part of an international space station which will eventually replace Mir.
